title: Public-Key Crypto

Public-Key Crypto

Many advanced CTF cryptography challenges involve RSA, elliptic-curve cryptography (ECC), ECDSA, lattices, or weak randomness.

Recommended tooling

  • SageMath for modular arithmetic, elliptic curves, and lattice reduction[1]
  • RsaCtfTool for testing common RSA weaknesses[2]
  • FactorDB for checking whether an integer has known factors[3]
  • The Python ecdsa library for key parsing, signing, and verification[7]

RSA

Start here when a challenge provides n, e, and c plus a hint such as a shared modulus, low exponent, partial key bits, or related messages.

rsa/README.md

ECC / ECDSA

If signatures are involved, test for nonce reuse, bias, or leakage before assuming that the underlying discrete-logarithm problem must be solved.

ECDSA nonce reuse / bias

ECDSA requires a fresh per-message secret number k. If the same k signs two different message hashes, the private key can be recovered from the public signature values.[4]

Even when k is not identical, bias or leakage of nonce bits across many signatures may enable lattice-based recovery.[5]

Technical recovery when k is reused:[4]

ECDSA signature equations (group order n):

  • r = (kG)_x mod n
  • s = k^{-1}(h(m) + r*d) mod n

If the same k is reused for two messages m1, m2 producing signatures (r, s1) and (r, s2):

  • k = (h(m1) - h(m2)) * (s1 - s2)^{-1} mod n
  • d = (s1*k - h(m1)) * r^{-1} mod n

Invalid-curve attacks

If a protocol fails to validate that an input point lies on the expected curve and in the correct subgroup, an attacker may force operations in a weaker group and recover information about a secret scalar. SEC 1 specifies public-key validation checks intended to prevent such inputs.[6]

Technical note:

  • Validate that points are not the point at infinity, have valid coordinates, satisfy the curve equation, and belong to the required subgroup.[6]
  • In CTF challenges, this is often modeled as a server multiplying an attacker-chosen point by a secret scalar and returning a derived value.

Malformed ML-DSA signing keys and rejection-sampling leakage

ML-DSA's expanded private key encodes polynomial vectors s1 and s2 with coefficients in [-η, η]. FIPS 204 notes that decoding malformed secret-key bytes can produce coefficients outside this range. The signing algorithm does not itself require an additional private-key consistency check.[8]

The relevant prerequisite is control over an expanded signing key before it is imported or used to sign, not a malformed public key submitted to a verifier. A permissive import path may accept altered packed coefficients and still produce signatures that verify. Compare acceptance at import and signing, then check the resulting signatures, using the cryptographic key-encoding fuzzing workflow.[9][10]

Signing computes z = y + c·s1 and r0 = LowBits(w − c·s2), rejecting a candidate when ||z||∞ ≥ γ1 − β or ||r0||∞ ≥ γ2 − β. These checks make accepted outputs independent of the valid small secrets. Out-of-range secret coefficients can upset that rejection-sampling argument and introduce secret-dependent bias. This is a conditional leakage mechanism, not a demonstrated full-key recovery from the reported library discrepancy.[8][10]

Private-key validation is distinct from signature verification. In the reported comparison, OpenSSL, BoringSSL, and SymCrypt applied extra private-key checks, while liboqs accepted malformed expanded keys during signing; its underlying mldsa-native provides a pk_from_sk() validator that liboqs did not expose. FIPS 204 does not mandate those extra validation checks.[9][10]
